description: In Active Voice, the subject performs the action, whereas in Passive Voice, the subject receives the action. This topic is crucial for sentence conversion, error spotting, and reading comprehension in competitive exams.

sections.title: Basic Concept of Voice
sections.description: Voice is the form of a verb that indicates whether the subject does the acting or is acted upon.

key_concepts.explanation: When the subject of the sentence performs the action. The sentence structure is subject-oriented and direct.
When the object of the active sentence becomes the subject, and the action is performed on it.

examples.correct_or_usage: A letter is written by Rohan. (Passive Voice)
examples.explanation: In the first sentence, Rohan (Subject) is doing the action. In the second, 'A letter' (Object) becomes the focus receiving the action.

sections.title: General Rules of Conversion
sections.description: Converting a sentence from Active to Passive requires following universally applicable structural rules.

grammar_rules.structure: Active Object -> Passive Subject | Active Subject -> 'by' + Passive Object
grammar_rules.explanation: The object of the active voice becomes the subject of the passive voice, and the active subject is placed at the end, typically preceded by the preposition 'by'.
Passive Voice always uses the third form of the main verb (Past Participle), regardless of the tense of the sentence.

key_concepts.explanation: Subjective pronouns must be converted to objective pronouns: I -> me, We -> us, You -> you, He -> him, She -> her, They -> them, It -> it.

examples.correct_or_usage: I am being helped by her. (Passive)
examples.explanation: 'me' changes to the subjective 'I', and 'She' changes to the objective 'her'. The main verb 'helping' becomes 'helped' (V3).

sections.title: Tense-Based Conversions
sections.description: Different tenses require specific helping verbs when converting to Passive Voice.

grammar_rules.structure: Present: is/are/am + V3 | Past: was/were + V3 | Future: will be/shall be + V3
grammar_rules.explanation: Indefinite tenses use 'To be' forms as helping verbs before the past participle.

grammar_rules.structure: Present: is/are/am + being + V3 | Past: was/were + being + V3
grammar_rules.explanation: Continuous tenses use 'being' to reflect the ongoing 'ing' action of the active verb.

grammar_rules.structure: Present: has/have + been + V3 | Past: had + been + V3 | Future: will have/shall have + been + V3
grammar_rules.explanation: Perfect tenses always incorporate 'been' before the past participle verb.

examples.incorrect_or_context: They had won the match. (Past Perfect Active)
examples.correct_or_usage: The match had been won by them. (Past Perfect Passive)
examples.explanation: The helping verb 'had' is followed by 'been' and the V3 form 'won'.

exceptions.explanation: In English grammar, 4 tenses cannot be converted into Passive Voice: Present Perfect Continuous, Past Perfect Continuous, Future Continuous, and Future Perfect Continuous.
exceptions.example: He has been reading since morning. (No Passive Form exists)

sections.title: Imperative and Interrogative Sentences
sections.description: Sentences containing commands, requests, or questions follow specific structural rules during conversion.

grammar_rules.structure: Let + Object + be + V3 OR You are requested/ordered/advised to + V1
grammar_rules.explanation: Commands use the 'Let' structure, while sentences with emotional tones use phrases like 'You are requested' depending on the context.

grammar_rules.structure: Helping Verb + Passive Subject + V3 + by + Passive Object + ?
grammar_rules.explanation: Questions remain questions in the passive form. 'Who' is specifically converted to 'By whom'.

examples.explanation: This is a command, so the 'Let...be+V3' structure is applied.

examples.correct_or_usage: By whom was this glass broken?
examples.explanation: 'Who' changes to 'By whom' and the Past Indefinite rule (was + V3) is followed.

sections.title: Exceptions and Special Cases
sections.description: Certain verbs and sentence structures bypass the standard 'by' rule or positional exchange rules.

exceptions.explanation: Some verbs do not take 'by' in the passive voice. They take fixed prepositions like: known to, surprised at, filled with, satisfied with.
exceptions.example: Active: I know him. -> Passive: He is known to me. (Never say 'known by me')

exceptions.explanation: When a sentence has both a Direct Object and an Indirect Object, either can become the subject in passive voice, though using the animate (indirect) object is generally preferred.
exceptions.example: Active: He gave me a pen. -> Passive: I was given a pen by him. OR A pen was given to me by him.

examples.correct_or_usage: I was surprised at his behavior.
examples.explanation: The verb 'surprise' is always followed by the preposition 'at', not 'by'.

sections.title: Strategies for Competitive Exams
sections.description: Mastering the art of option elimination saves time and boosts accuracy in multiple-choice questions.

strategies.title: Identify the Tense First
strategies.detail: Unlike Direct-Indirect speech, the tense NEVER changes in Voice conversion. If the active sentence is in Present, the passive must be in Present. Eliminate options that change the tense immediately.

strategies.title: Check for the V3 Form
strategies.detail: Ensure the correct option features the main verb in its third form (Past Participle). Options lacking a V3 verb are definitively incorrect.

strategies.title: Verify Subject-Verb Agreement
strategies.detail: Check if the new subject (formerly the object) is singular or plural, and verify that the helping verb correctly matches this new subject's number.
